caseno: Writ Petition No 422 of 1994 with Writ Petition No. 1685 of 1997 with Writ Petition No. 1649 of 1996 with Writ Petition No. 1650 of 1996 with Writ Petition No. 2355 of 1995.
lawyer:
MA Latiff Majumder, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner 
Mahbubul Haque, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No. 2
parties:
Rupali Bank Ltd ------ Petitioner
vs
Chairman 2nd Labour Court Dhaka & another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
5. In these cases the respondent State claimed all benefits of permanent workers from the date of joining after they were appointed. The petitioner Bank appeared in the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka (respondent No. 1) and contested the cases by filing written statement denying all the materials allegations which were made in the applications and stated, inter alia, that the petitions in the Labour Court were not maintainable under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965 as they were barred by limitation. The respondents were also not workers under the petitioner and, as such, had no locus standi to file the complaint cases. The respondent has served grievance petition after many years i.e. after the cause of action arose, instead of filing the same within 15 days of the cause of action i.e. 3 (three) months after the date of joining when they claim their right to be treated as permanent workers. The petitioner submitted that the respondents were appointed purely on temporary basis in temporary projects and they were the employees of the loan borrowers of the Bank. The respondents were never employees of the petitioner. They were appointed for different borrowers and there was no master and servant relationship between the present`s petitioner and the respondent No. 2 in the Writ Petitions. These respondents used to work in the projects of the borrower and after the liquidation of their loan for the project, their services would terminate automatically and in this way they continued their service in different projects of different borrowers in different god own. They used to belong to the pay roll of different borrowers and, as such, the petitioner had no liability whatsoever for their pay and allowances or for payment of bonus and provident fund, etc. The borrowers of the Bank used to pay their salary and also bonus, etc. On humanitarian grounds on certain occasions such as Eid festivals, they were paid festival bonus which was never the concern of the petitioner. The petitioner on the request of different borrowers recruited these respondents on the basis of no work no pay against definite project to be paid by the borrower from borrower's account and the borrowers used to bear the pay and allowances of the respondents. 

 10. The net submissions made by the learned Counsel for the petitioner is that, the grievance petitions filed by the respondents and the complaint cases filed under section 25 of the Standing Orders Act, 1965 were hopelessly barred by limitation fixed by the said section of the Act. In support of his contention the learned Counsel has referred is to section 25 of the Employment of Labour Standing Orders, Act 1965. He says that admittedly the respondents No.2 were appointed in the 1970s and 1980s and they filed their grievance petitions in 1993 and 1994 i.e. several years after they claim to have become permanent workers after successfully completing of 3 (three) months of service after their date of joining. It may be convenient to quote section 25 of the Act, which relates to grievance procedure. It reads: 

 13. These decisions are also supported by the decision reported in (Abul Kalam vs Labour Court) 38 DLR 399. The learned Counsel for the petitioner has submitted that rightly or wrongly if the respondents have not been paid their benefit as permanent worker for so many years this cannot be said to be a grievance coming within the purview of section 25 of the Standing Orders Act, 1965. He compared the non-payment of benefit of a permanent worker similar to retirement from the service against which no grievance lies. In this connection he has referred to the case of Adamjee Jute Mills vs Chairman 3rd Court reported in 42 DLR 275 in which the High Court considered the question whether retirement from the service was a grievance coming within the purview of section 25 of the Act. It was held that since the retirement right or wrong is not covered under any of the provisions of the Act as grievance, the workers so retired cannot invoke the jurisdiction of the Labour Court. Finally, he has submitted an unreported decision of the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1987 and Criminal Appeal No. 12 of 1990 in which the Appellate Division held that the Labour Court is not a civil Court although it might have trappings of some of it. Being a Special Court it must follow the limitation set by the Labour Court. 

 "As regards the third point Mr Shafique Ahmed has reformulated it in a different way before us. He contends that the benefit under section 34 of the Ordinance extending to an individual Worker was extended to him, if at all, when the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 was amended on the 17th October, 1970 and on that date his right of termination benefit under section 19 of the Standing Orders Act had become barred, and so the right itself was extinguished. There was, therefore, no such right secured under the law available to the worker for enforcement when the said section came into existence and when the application was filed on 9-11-70. This argument though ingenious, yet it does not stand the scrutiny of reasoning. Firstly, we are applying provisions of section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance which is a different enactment and there is no such bar of limitation therein as has been contended. Secondly, the argument is fallacious in view of the fact that under the provisions of the Standing Orders Act what was barred was the remedy under it, but the rights secured to a worker under section 19 were not extinguished. There is a great distinction between the barring of a remedy and extinguishment of a right. Nothing could be found in Standing Orders Act to read that after the prescribed period under section 25 the right secured under the Act also be extinguished. There being no such express, bar, the ordinary principle of the interpretation of Statutes will apply. The Rule is that limitation restricts rights to take legal action for enforcement of an existing right after the lapse of certain period. It does not extinguish the right but simply bars the enforcement of the said right after certain lapse of time. We find that the right survived and the Ordinance secured to the worker that right and also gave him remedy for its enforcement without prescribing any period of limitation. The point advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner fails." 

 15. We will first consider the decisions of the High Court Division in the above mentioned case of Howlader Jute Mills Ltd and Deputy Managing Director National Bank of Pakistan both reported in 28 DLR on which the petitioner relies. In the first case in which an amendment of the petition was allowed by the Labour Court, it was found that their services were terminated because of their trade union activities. Their grievance was not brought to the notice of the employer within the time limit prescribed in section 25 of the Standing Orders Act. The amendment having been allowed it was to be deemed that a new case was filed on that day, which was time barred. In the second case the grievance of non-payment of subsistence allowance was beyond time. After the grievance arose in the National Bank case the employee had right to the grievance on 1-6-67 when the Bank replied to his application for subsistence allowance but the respondent (employee) did not take any step till after more than 2 years when he filed representation purported to be his grievance petition on 7-10-69 and thereafter filed the case under section 25 on 22-11-69. From the facts and circumstances discussed above it is clear that the petitioner's cause of grievance arose on the following month of his suspension in August, 1966 when he was not paid any subsistence allowance, and the case was filed more than 3 years after i.e. on 22-11-69. We find that in both the cases representation for redress were made beyond the limitation of time under section 25 of the Act. Therefore, we are in agreement with the decisions in those two cases. The limitation as fixed or imposed by section 25 of the Standing Orders Act was rightly applied in those cases. We will now have to see in the facts and circumstances of the case before us whether the decisions in those two cases are applicable. It was argued for the petitioner that although in the case of Omar sons Ltd it was said that section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance did not prescribe any period of limitation and right which does not extinguish can be enforced under the said section, in the instant cases even if the right might not have extinguished, since section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act prescribes a period of limitation this right cannot be enforced under Section 25. However we find that the facts and circumstances in the case of Omar sons Ltd are different from the cases before us. The service of the worker in Omar sons Ltd was terminated and therefore the right of endorsement had become time barred under section 25 of the Act. In the instant cases the respondents No. 2 are still in the service of the petitioner Rupali Bank and therefore, their rights attached to their service are continuing rights and the non-payment of benefits of a permanent worker is a continuous breach of an obligation under law his a continuing wrong giving rise to continuous cause of action. Therefore, the limitation under section 25 of the Standing Orders Act is not applicable in the present case and section 23 of the Limitation Act will be applicable. Mr Mahbubul Hoque the learned Counsel for the respondents No. 2 has referred us to section 23 of the Limitation Act and two decision in cases similar to the present case and different from the cases reported in 28 DLR section 23 of the Limitation Act provides: 

 "In the case of a continuing breach of contract and in the case of a continuing wrong independent of contract, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during, which the breach or the wrong, as the case may be continues," 

 17. A similar view was taken in the case of Sarat Chandra vs Nirod Chandra reported in AIR 1935 (Cal) 405. It was held that where the plaintiff has a right to use the land on which certain sheds have been erected as a passage and those sheds are obstructing his passage way there is a continuing wrong and a suit for declaration of plaintiffs right to use the land and for removal of sheds is governed by section 23 of the Limitation Act the High Court of Calcutta held. 

 18. In the instant cases the non-consideration by the petitioner that the respondents No. 2 were its permanent workers and entitled to get all the benefits of a permanent worker are continuous wrongs and, as such, it is our view that a fresh period of limitation began to run at every moment of the time during which the petitioner continued with the wrong. In these cases the wrong was the non-consideration of the respondents being permanent workers and non-payment of the benefits of a permanent worker. It has been argued by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that the provision of the Limitation Act is not applicable in the instant case as this is governed by special law. The Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965 is a special law and only the limitation imposed by section 25 of the said Act is applicable in the present cases. At the very outset we must express our view that section 25 does not set any limit in cases where there is a continuous breach of contract or a continuous wrong done by the employer against the existing employees. In Omar sons Ltd case to which we have referred above, the service of the worker was terminated and therefore, if the service of the respondents No. 2 had been terminated then there would not have been a continuous breach or wrong and in which case limitation set under section 25 of the Act would have been applicable, but in the instant case admittedly the respondents are still in service and therefore there is no break in the wrong and the grievance continues. We may refer to the case of Secretary Bangladesh Jute Corporation vs Chairman, 2nd Labour Court reported in 41 DLR 265. It was submitted that the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965 being a Special law section 14 of the Limitation Act has no application. Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, as he then was, observed: 

 "This submissions has no legs to stand. Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act provides as follows: 

 "Where any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefore by the First Schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefore in that Schedule and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special law". 

 (b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply. Therefore, section 14 of the Limitation Act has full force and application and the 2nd Labour Court at Dhaka did not act without jurisdiction in entertaining the complaint case." 

 19. In the instant cases section 23 of the Limitation Act has not expressly been excluded by the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and in the absence of any limitation provided by section 25 in the case of continuous breach or wrong, section 23 of the Limitation Act will have full force and application and the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka, was not without jurisdiction in entertaining the above complaint cases. In the facts and circumstances of the cases we also find that the two unreported judgments of the Appellate Division referred to by the learned Counsel for the petitioner have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present cases.
